caption:
A false positive is not free. It is a patrol diverted, a crew sent to a site with nothing there, hours of exposure for zero yield.

Most pitches for monitoring systems talk about detection rate — how much it catches. Few talk about the other number: how often a flag turns out to be nothing. A system that flags everything catches everything too, and burns out the people who have to check each one.

The real measure of a collection system is not sensitivity alone. It is sensitivity weighed against the cost of acting on a flag that doesn't pan out. Confidence grading exists to carry that weight — so a low-confidence flag gets a different response than a confirmed one, not the same scramble every time.
thread: A false positive is not free. It is a patrol sent out, fuel burned, hours of exposure, for a site where nothing was there.
Detection rate gets the attention. Precision — how often a flag is real — gets ignored. A system that flags everything catches everything, and exhausts whoever has to check it.
The fix isn't fewer flags. It's grading them. Confirmed, assessed, and uncertain calls draw different responses, not the same scramble every time.
Cost of a missed event and cost of a false alarm are different numbers. Treating them as the same number is how good systems get ignored.

card.headline: A flag that's wrong still costs fuel
card.sub: Every dispatched patrol on a false alarm is a real cost. Grading confidence, not just counting flags, is what keeps a system worth acting on.

rationale: Covers an unaddressed EXPLAINER angle — the operational cost of false positives and precision vs. raw detection — teaching a concrete concept without repeating prior cadence/radar/confidence posts.
